[Q&A] How to implement default TTS for speak in an adapter?

nodes.body:
Good questions, and they land on a real seam in the example. Answers in order.

**Q1, is `GoPiGo3Adapter(speak=None)` the right way to get espeak.** Yes. `__init__` does `self._speak = speak or _espeak`, so `speak=None` (or omitting it) resolves to the built-in `_espeak`; passing `spoken.append` is what overrides it. The committed `run_gopigo3.py` passes `spoken.append` on purpose, so the demo report is deterministic and byte-asserted in CI, not because that is the deployment shape. On your Pi, `GoPiGo3Adapter()` with no `speak=` is correct.

One thing on your espeak-ng call. Keep the list form the existing `_espeak` uses and drop `shell=True`: `subprocess.run(["espeak-ng", utterance], check=False)`. Your version, `subprocess.run(['espeak-ng "%s"' % utterance], shell=True)`, interpolates the utterance into a shell string, which breaks on quotes in the text and is an injection path. The list form needs neither.

**Q2, should speak actually speak without `--execute`.** Your instinct matches the project's. The catch: the fake/real backend swap only gates the wheels, because it replaces `easygopigo3`. Speech goes through `self._speak`, a separate path, so wiring espeak as the default makes it talk even in a dry run. That contradicts validate-before-actuate and the safe-by-default posture the `--execute` flag exists for. The fix that mirrors the wheels: thread the `prefer_real` flag to the speech backend, capture (`spoken.append`) in a dry run and emit (`_espeak`) only under `--execute`. Speech is an actuation; gate it like one. This is example code, so no RFC needed; a good thing to fold into your PR.

**Q3, pointing tts_engine_class at piper-tts when hyphens are not valid function names.** The premise has two parts to untangle. First, `tts_engine_class` is a closed vocabulary in the Layer-1 HAL: `openvoice | piper | mozilla_tts | espeak | custom`. So you declare `piper`, not `piper-tts`, and `espeak` covers espeak-ng. If you need to name the exact binary, use `custom` and put the string in `tts_engine_class_note` (the validator requires the note when the class is `custom`). Second, that manifest value never becomes a Python function name. It is an advisory declaration; the adapter decides how to map it. Use a dispatch dict, `{"espeak": _espeak, "piper": _piper}`, keyed by the declared class, and a hyphenated real binary lives in the subprocess args or as a dict key, never as an identifier. Note URML already flags that piper is GPL-3.0, so run it across a subprocess boundary rather than importing it. Declaring the class only silences the `capability.tts_engine_undeclared` warning; the adapter is still what actually picks the engine at runtime.

— Ido

> a good thing to fold into your PR.

Not sure how to do that - sorry to be such a beggar.  Would really like the GoPiGo3 runtime example to be something worth others learning from.

You're not a beggar at all. This is exactly the kind of feedback that makes the example better, so thank you.

I went ahead and folded all three into the canonical example, so you don't have to wrestle with a PR. It's on main now (#599). Pull it into your fork and diff against what you have.

What changed:

Q1: the default backend now prefers espeak-ng and falls back to espeak. It keeps the list-argument form on purpose, `subprocess.run(["espeak-ng", utterance])`, with no `shell=True`, so quotes in the text stay literal and there's no injection path.

Q2, the important one: speech is now gated like the wheels. You were right that it shouldn't talk in a dry run. The fake/real swap only covered easygopigo3, so speech had its own ungated path. The runner now captures the utterance on a dry run and only lets espeak speak under `--execute`. Speech is an actuation, so it's gated like one.

Q3: the adapter now takes a `tts_engine_class` and maps it through a small dispatch dict, `{"espeak": _espeak}`. To add piper, write a `_piper(utterance)` that shells out to it and add it under the `"piper"` key. The hyphenated binary lives in the subprocess args, never as a function name. Declare `piper` in the manifest, or `custom` with a note for an exact binary.

On your Pi, `GoPiGo3Adapter()` with no `speak=` now gives you real espeak-ng under `--execute`, and silence (captured) on a dry run, which is what you were after.

Credit is yours for spotting the dry-run-speech gap. It was a real one.

-- Ido
Thanks - tried it on Dave, works great

That's the report I was hoping for. Seeing it run right on Dave, on real hardware, is the whole point.

Thanks for pushing on it. The example is better because you did, and the next person who wires up a GoPiGo3 gets the fixed version.

nodes.title: [Q&A]  GoPiGo3 Prompting and Manifest Validation For "Orbit 180 degrees with a 5 cm radius"

nodes.body:
Good question, and chasing it down I found this is a bug on our side, not a prompting problem. Thanks for the detailed repro; it made the fix obvious.

The short version: your LLM was right and the adapter was wrong.

Per RFC-0630, which defines `drive`, `distance` is the path length in metres traveled along the curve, and `arc` is the degrees swept over it. The radius is implied: radius = distance / arc-in-radians. So "orbit 180 degrees with a 5 cm radius" is a 0.157 m arc (pi x 0.05):

```yaml
- drive:
    distance: 0.157   # arc length = radius x angle = 0.05 m x pi
    arc: 180
```

That 0.157 is exactly the number your qwen run produced. The model reasoned correctly that `distance` is arc length. Its real mistakes were the swept angle (it emitted -90 instead of 180) and splitting the orbit into turn+drive steps, both of which are promptable.

The bug: in `gopigo3_adapter.py`, `drive_by` was passing `distance` straight in as the orbit radius:

```python
radius_cm = abs(cm)          # cm = distance * 100
gpg.orbit(arc, radius_cm)
```

That contradicts RFC-0630, so even a perfect program came out at the wrong radius. Your `orbit(-90, 15.7)` should have been radius = 0.157 / (pi/2) = 0.10 m, i.e. `orbit(-90, 10)`. The corrected line:

```python
radius_cm = abs(cm) / abs(math.radians(arc))
```

The fix is up in PR #580 with a regression test. Once it lands, `drive: {distance: 0.157, arc: 180}` drives Dave in a true 5 cm-radius half circle; I ran it end to end and it lowers to `orbit(180.0, 5.0)`.

For prompting after the fix, a 9B model gets there with one hint plus one example: "For a curved drive, `arc` is the degrees swept and `distance` is the path length in metres along the arc (radius x angle in radians)." Then show it "orbit 90 degrees with 20 cm radius" -> `drive: {arc: 90, distance: 0.314}`.

That is the second real bug Dave has surfaced, and again one that only shows up on a real robot. Thank you.

— Ido

### Summary:
- Great progress with the system prompt to LLM generating good URML for a phrase targeting orbits.
- Good progress getting radius to the orbit in the runtime
- ISSUE: The radii are 2x the requested values. 

Here is Lyrical Dave executing the URML:

https://youtu.be/Cpw7N6mznMo

drive_distance = math.pi * abs(radius) * abs(degrees) / 180 # / 180 is shorter than radius * 2 / 360

so that seems to match what the LLM is putting out.

Great catch, and you did the hard part by pinning it to the number. Short version: the adapter is doing the right thing, and the 2x is coming out of the model, not the runtime.

Walk the 5 cm case through:

- "orbit 180 degrees, 5 cm radius" -> the true arc length is `pi x 0.05 = 0.157 m`. That is what `distance` should be.
- qwen put out `distance: 0.314, arc: 180`. And `0.314` is `2 x 0.157`. It doubled, effectively using the diameter where it wanted the radius, a classic r-vs-d slip.
- The adapter then inverts that faithfully: `radius_cm = 31.4 / radians(180) = 31.4 / 3.14159 = 10.0`. Given a 0.314 m arc swept over 180 degrees, `orbit(180, 10)` is the mathematically correct call. So the runtime is not the bug here; it is honestly reporting a doubled input.

You can confirm the runtime is right by feeding it the correct number by hand. `distance: 0.157, arc: 180` lowers to `orbit(180, 5.0)`. Your 10 cm step is the same story: qwen gave `0.629`, which is `2 x 0.314`, and it lowered to `orbit(180, 20.0)`.

So there are two separate things here:

1. Immediate. The 9B model is losing a factor of 2 on the arc-length arithmetic. A stronger model, or a system-prompt line that spells out `arc_length = radius x angle_in_radians` (not diameter, not full circumference), should clear the symptom.

2. The deeper point, which is on us. Encoding a curved drive as (path-length, degrees) forces the model to compute `r x theta` every single time, and that is exactly where a small model drops a 2. The two numbers a person actually says out loud are the radius and the sweep angle. If `drive` accepted those directly, say `drive: {radius: 0.05, arc: 180}` as an alternative to `{distance, arc}`, the model would pass through the numbers it was handed with no trig at all, and the adapter would call `orbit(arc, radius)` straight. That removes the whole class of error rather than hoping the model gets the multiplication right.

That second one touches how `drive` is specified (RFC-0630), so it is a Layer-2 change and I am taking it to the maintainer as a possible RFC rather than quietly patching it. Either way, you found a real seam. Thank you, and no apology owed on the Pi. You did the calculus that mattered.

Here is Dave's run for anyone following: https://youtu.be/Cpw7N6mznMo

-- Ido

Shipped. Your finding turned into RFC-0665, and it is on main now.

You can write that orbit as the radius and the angle directly, the two numbers the instruction actually gives:

```yaml
- drive:
    radius: 0.05
    arc: 180
```

The runtime resolves that to the same arc internally (`distance = radius x radians(arc)`), so there is no arithmetic left for the model to get wrong, and it lowers to `easygopigo3.orbit(180, 5.0)`. The old form (`distance` + `arc`) still works unchanged; the radius form is just the arithmetic-free way to name the same arc. The validator also bounds it by the arc length it travels, not the radius, so `max_relative_distance` still means what it says.

I also added a bridge few-shot on your exact phrasing ("orbit 180 degrees with a 5 cm radius"), so a model that sees a radius and a sweep angle now emits the radius form instead of computing an arc length. That is the factor-of-2 gone at the source rather than papered over.

Thanks for pinning it to the number. That is what made the fix obvious, and it is a better fix than the one I would have written if you had only said "it drives wrong."

-- Ido

Dave made three **clockwise** rotations of 180 degrees with the correct radii  - alas the easygopigo3.orbit() does not follow the Forward-Left-Up convention of ROS and URML:

```easygopigo3.orbit(degrees, radius_cm=0, blocking=True)
        :param int degrees: Degrees to steer. **360** for full rotation. Negative for left turn.
```

I have forked the URML repo and taking a stab at getting the speak and wait_passively primitives working - almost ready to submit a PR for review.  I'm going to split the "slimey" issue I filed against the GoPiGo3 runtime, and will add a third issue to correct the drive-arc degrees sign specific to the GoPiGo3 API.

Right call splitting it out, and the handedness belongs exactly where you are putting it: in the adapter, not the program.

URML and ROS are Forward-Left-Up, so a positive `arc` (or `turn` angle) is counterclockwise, left. `easygopigo3.orbit(degrees, radius_cm)` reads the opposite: per its own docstring, negative is a left turn, positive is clockwise. So `drive_by` handing `arc` straight to `orbit` inverts the sign, which is why Dave went clockwise on a positive arc. The clean fix is to negate at the substrate boundary in `gopigo3_adapter.py`, `gpg.orbit(-arc, radius_cm)`, so the URML stays FLU and the adapter owns the vendor convention. Worth checking `turn_degrees` the same way while you are in there; if its positive is also clockwise, `turn_by` needs the same negation.

Keeping that sign map inside the adapter is the point of the layer split: the program a person writes never depends on one vendor library's rotation convention. Send the speak and wait_passively PR whenever it is ready and I will review it.

— Ido

nodes.body:
Thanks for flagging this, it is worth watching, and it is a good sign rather than a threat. Independent people converging on "there should be a standard layer between the LLM and the robot" is the whole premise.

ClawsJoy landed on the same split we did. Their 12 primitives bound to ROS topics are a substrate binding, the "how to execute" layer. URML sits above as the intent layer: "what to do," validated against a capability manifest before anything actuates. They said as much in the thread, sketching NL to LLM to URML intent to their bridge to ROS 2. That is exactly how the layers are meant to compose, and it is the cleanest outside articulation of it I have seen.

Two things that split gives URML a reason to exist for: the validate-before-actuate gate (nothing runs until it is checked against the robot's declared capabilities and safety envelope), and substrate independence (their primitives assume ROS topics; a GoPiGo3 with no ROS, like Dave, still runs URML). A fixed primitive list on ROS is a fine Layer-0/1 target for URML to compile down to.

I may go say hello on that thread. Good find.

Done, and thank you for the nudge.
There is now a native, non-ROS GoPiGo3 example runtime in the repo: examples/gopigo3/ (landing in PR #532).

It has three pieces:
a basic GoPiGo3 manifest (differential, relative-motion, a distance sensor, an espeak output),
a GoPiGo3Adapter that drives the wheels through easygopigo3 (drive_cm, turn_degrees, orbit) and speaks through espeak,
and a runner that validates a program and then executes it through the adapter.

The headline case is the exact command you translated: announce "Driving forward 1 meter", then drive 1 m.
It validates, then calls easygopigo3.drive_cm(100.0) on the wheels.
A short patrol (turn, drive, turn, drive, announce, report) is in there too.

It runs here against a fake easygopigo3 so CI stays hermetic, and unchanged on your Pi once you pip install gopigo3 easygopigo3 and delete the fake block.
drive and turn map to your encoders; "announce" maps to speak, which the Pi backs with espeak.
A basic GoPiGo3 has no arm or camera, so grasp / detect / capture come back as not-supported rather than faked; you extend the adapter to add them.

If you send your gopigo3.manifest.yaml I will tune the example to match your exact distances and speeds.

Thanks,

nodes.body:
Good question, and your instinct at the end is correct: it is a loop, not a single call.

What emit-prompt gives you is the system message. The actual prompt urml translate sends is a normal two-message chat call:

role: system = the emit-prompt output (schema + your manifest + envelope + profile few-shots)
role: user = your instruction string, e.g. Announce 'Executing a URML program'
So nothing is hidden. 
The "real prompt" is just those two messages. One correction on your env: OPENAI_API_KEY=qwen3.5:9b is putting the model where the key goes. 
The model name belongs in the request body, and Ollama ignores the key entirely (any value works).

A bash script that reproduces attempt 1 with curl:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

INSTRUCTION="Announce 'Executing a URML program'"

# The system message. Add --include-few-shots so it matches what
# `urml translate` actually sends (translate includes profile few-shots).
urml emit-prompt \
  --manifest your.manifest.yaml \
  --profile educational \
  --include-few-shots \
  --out system_prompt.txt

SYSTEM=$(jq -Rs . < system_prompt.txt)
USER=$(jq -Rs . <<< "$INSTRUCTION")

curl -sS "${OPENAI_BASE_URL}/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${OPENAI_API_KEY:-ollama}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{
    \"model\": \"qwen3.5:9b\",
    \"messages\": [
      {\"role\": \"system\", \"content\": ${SYSTEM}},
      {\"role\": \"user\",   \"content\": ${USER}}
    ],
    \"response_format\": {\"type\": \"json_object\"},
    \"stream\": false
  }"
Now the part you guessed right. That curl is one POST, 
which is exactly attempt 1. If the model's first emission passes validation, that is the whole translate, one round trip. 
If it does not, the bridge takes the validator's structured errors, appends them to the system prompt as revision context, and asks again, up to 3 times by default. curl alone will not do that validate-then-revise loop; running the loop is the entire reason the bridge exists. 
So your "this would not work as a single request" is correct: a single request is only the happy path where the model gets it right the first time.

(And yes, good instinct flagging the three-week-old account.)

Two things: a correction you earned, and the real cause of the 34 minutes.

First, you are right and my script was wrong. There is no `--include-few-shots`; few-shots are on by default, and `--no-few-shots` drops them. Thanks for the catch. That flag turns out to be the lever for your actual problem, which is the nice part.

Now the 34 minutes. It is not a cold start. Your `ollama ps` shows the model resident the whole time, keep-alive refreshing, never reloading. The clue is in the response you printed: `prompt_tokens: 20071`. You prefilled a twenty-thousand-token prompt through a 9B model at 100% CPU, no GPU. That prefill is the wall, not the network and not a timeout. The model then generated only 79 tokens, which is the fast part. So the same thing is happening under `urml translate`: it is not hanging, it is grinding through 20k tokens of prompt on the CPU.

That reframes the timeout question from before. `URML_OPENAI_TIMEOUT=600` would not even cover a 34-minute prefill; raising the timeout just stops the error, it does not make it fast. The thing to drive down is prompt tokens, or move the prefill onto a GPU.

Levers, most effective first:
1. A GPU, even a modest one. CPU prefill of a 20k prompt on a 9B is tens of minutes; on a GPU it is seconds. This is the real fix if you have the hardware.
2. Shrink the prompt. `urml emit-prompt --no-few-shots` (and the same omission inside translate) drops the few-shot examples, which are a big chunk of those 20k tokens. You trade some first-try reliability for a much shorter prefill. The program JSON schema is also large and less removable, so do not expect it to get tiny, but cutting few-shots is the easy win.
3. Drop `num_ctx`. You are running 128000 context; Ollama sizes its KV cache to that, which on CPU is pure overhead when your prompt is 20k. Set it to something like 32768, still well above your prompt, and you reclaim memory and some speed.

A smaller model prefills faster, but you already found 9B is the first that translates clean, so that is a real tradeoff rather than a free win.

Short version: it was never cold start or a flaky timeout. It is a 20k-token prompt meeting a CPU. Cut the tokens or feed it a GPU.

Good news, and it turns on exactly the thing you are asking about.

The retries should be much faster than that first 34 minutes, not three more full prefills. Here is why: when the bridge revises, it appends the revision text (the prior emission plus the validator errors) to the very end of the prompt. Everything before it, the manifest, the envelope, the examples, and the big JSON schema that makes up the bulk of your 20k tokens, is byte-identical from attempt to attempt. A resident Ollama reuses the prefill for that shared prefix (llama.cpp keeps the last KV cache and reuses the longest common prefix), so a retry only has to prefill the short appended revision block plus your instruction, then generate. Expect retries in a fraction of the first time, as long as the model stays loaded between attempts, which it does because the bridge fires them back to back, and Ollama's prompt cache is on, which is the default.

One important detail on the timeout: `URML_OPENAI_TIMEOUT` is per request, not per translate. So 2400 comfortably covers the 34-minute first attempt and each faster retry. The worst case is first-prefill plus three short retries, not four times 34 minutes.

And the part that matters most: in your curl test the first emission already validated. That means zero retries. Revisions only fire when validation fails, which for a clean instruction against a good manifest is the exception, not the rule. So most of your runs are one 34-minute attempt and done. The one lever that speeds up that first attempt specifically is `--no-few-shots`, since caching only helps the retries, not the first prefill.

nodes.title: [Q&A] How do I run a URML primitive test on my robot?

nodes.body:
There are two different paths here.

For a GoPiGo3 smoke test, the direct path is still the example runner. It is dry-run by default, and `-f` lets you point it at your own translated URML file:

```bash
python examples/gopigo3/run_gopigo3.py -f my-program.urml.yaml
python examples/gopigo3/run_gopigo3.py -f my-program.urml.yaml --execute
```

The second command is the one that can move a connected GoPiGo3. The runner does not currently expose a `test_emit_speech` subcommand in the source I checked; it loads either the built-in demos or the file passed with `-f`. For a speech-only test, the clean version is a tiny URML file with one `speak` step and then running it with `-f`.

The conformance suite is useful, but it is a runtime/adapter contract test, not a single-primitive hardware button. To run it against real hardware, you need a zero-argument adapter factory, then:

```bash
python -m urml_conformance --adapter your_module:make_adapter --filter educational
```

where `make_adapter()` returns a fresh adapter instance each time. If you omit `--adapter`, it uses the hermetic mock adapter, so no robot is touched.

One more practical detail: the current educational fixtures are mostly navigation-style patrol cases plus minimal-node output cases. They are good for checking an educational runtime shape, but they are not the same thing as "just test speech on my GoPiGo3." For that, I would use the GoPiGo3 runner with a one-step `speak` program first; add or propose a conformance fixture only if you want that behavior pinned as part of the shared educational profile contract.

@cookesan has this exactly right, thank you for jumping in.

To confirm and add one practical note: there is no test_emit_speech subcommand. 
The clean way to smoke-test a single primitive is a tiny URML file with one step and the example runner, which is dry-run by default:


# one speak step in speak-test.urml.yaml, then:
python examples/gopigo3/run_gopigo3.py -f speak-test.urml.yaml            # validates + plans, no movement
python examples/gopigo3/run_gopigo3.py -f speak-test.urml.yaml --execute  # actually speaks/moves
Always run it once without --execute first to see the planned calls, then add --execute when you are ready. 
Same pattern for a one-step drive or turn.

Ido

nodes.title: URML in the "Mind of an autonomous robot"

nodes.body:
This is the right distinction, and it is worth being precise about.

URML is not the mastermind. It is the intent-to-validated-action layer, and the mastermind sits above it.
In your example, the part that decides "it is activity hours, the battery is over 50%, so wander and look for unclassified shapes" is autonomy: a planner, a behavior tree, a policy, your own Python. That loop owns perception, classification, and the choice of what to do next.

What URML gives that loop is a safe, checkable verb for each action it wants to take.
"Drive forward a bit", "turn to a new heading", "take a picture and tag it with time and pose", "store it here" become URML primitives, each validated against the robot's manifest and safety envelope before it runs. The mastermind proposes; URML refuses anything the robot cannot do or is not allowed to do, then executes what passes.

So the split for your patrol is:
the wandering, the shape detection, and the "is this already classified" judgment stay in your autonomy code,
and each concrete motion or capture it decides on goes through URML as a validated step.
A couple of those, "detect a shape" and "store tagged photos", are perception and IO that a basic robot does not declare yet, so they would come back as not-supported until the manifest and an adapter cover them. That boundary is the useful part: the mastermind can be as creative as it likes, and the robot still only does what was declared possible and checked safe.

Happy to sketch how a slice of that patrol would look as URML steps if that would help.

Thanks,
Ido

Two followup thoughts:
1) Is there a mechanism to pause/resume and a mechanism to cancel mid-urml-sequence with summary of executed primitives or step identifier?

2) How do you envision the "deconflict my presence" behaviors (single urml? multiple urml?):
> begin moving on the deconflict path very slowly at first ensuring the path deconfliction remains valid. If the object/human's path changes to deconflict faster, continue motion at the slow pace, otherwise slowly accelerate motion till the deconflict target location is reached.

I went ahead and built the sketch as a runnable example, since the boundary is easier to see in code than in prose: examples/autonomy-boundary/ (PR #535).

It plays a plain-Python Mastermind through your patrol.
The mastermind owns the decisions: the activity-hours and battery-over-50% gate, where to wander, the "is this an unclassified shape?" judgment, and storing the tagged photos. URML expresses none of that.
Each physical action it decides on becomes a validated URML step: turn, drive, capture, then a distance measure. The whole patrol validates and runs through the mock substrate.

The interesting part is the boundary the other way.
When the mastermind tries to push its perception judgment down into URML as detect(object: unclassified_shape), the validator refuses it with capability.missing_object_class. Novelty detection is not a declared capability, so it stays in autonomy where it belongs.

That is the whole point in one line: the mastermind can be as clever as it likes, and the robot still only does what the manifest declares and the envelope allows.
Have a look and tell me if the split matches how you think about Carl and Dave's autonomy.

Thanks,
Ido

I guess the vendor owning the "robot xyz runtime" will determine what hooks into and out of the specific runtime are implemented - concepts of interruption with completion report, monitoring progress, start/stop times, replanning a path under the path follower, altering a primitive's parameter (like speed, altering a final heading between start of motion and a completion condition)

I saw "parallel" mentioned somewhere - I think that might clear up some fog.

Eventually, will want to learn about the TurtleBot4 ROS runtime, I saw mentioned.  Although Dave is a ROS bot, there will never be a vendor ROS runtime, so my TB5-WaLI turtlebot4 clone may be better there.

These are the right questions, and they land almost exactly on the line between URML and the runtime, which you already put your finger on in your second note. Let me take them in turn.

**Cancel, and a report of what ran.** Today URML gives you the report, not an external pause. Every behavior runs under an `on_error` policy (`abort_and_report`, `continue`, or `retry`). When a step fails or the program aborts, the runtime returns a result carrying `steps_executed`, the full audit log of which primitives ran and in what order, and the last outcome. So you do get the "summary of executed primitives" on an abort. What URML does not yet define is an operator-initiated pause/resume or a cancel-from-outside mid-sequence. That is deliberate for now, and it is exactly the runtime-hook territory you describe: it belongs to the vendor runtime's lifecycle, not to the language. A small, neutral lifecycle and progress contract any runtime could implement (cancel, pause, a progress event, a step identifier) is a real open design question, and the kind of thing that would go through an RFC rather than get bolted on quietly.

**You are right about runtime hooks.** Interruption with a completion report, progress monitoring, start and stop times, replanning under a path follower, altering a primitive's parameter mid-motion: those are runtime capabilities, and which ones exist depends on the runtime the vendor ships. URML's job is to say what the validated intent is; the runtime's job is to execute, monitor, and interrupt it. Keeping that line clean is what lets one program run on a GoPiGo3, a TurtleBot, or a drone without rewriting.

**`parallel` is the piece you were missing.** URML Layer 3 has four composition nodes: `sequence`, `branch`, `parallel`, and `retry`. `parallel` runs several behaviors at once with a join policy, `complete_when: all` (wait for every branch), `any` (succeed when any does), or `first_to_succeed` (race them and stop the rest). That is the lever for your deconfliction case.

**The deconfliction behavior.** I would model it as: declare the goal and the bounds in URML, and let a monitor govern the motion. The move toward the deconflict point is one validated step, capped by the safety envelope's speed limit and the operational-clearance volume URML already declares for separation (RFC-0291). The "go slowly, accelerate only while the path stays clear" logic is a closed reactive loop, which is a controller, so it lives in the runtime or your autonomy. `parallel` binds them: run the motion alongside a `wait_for` that watches the deconfliction condition, with `first_to_succeed`, so the instant separation is at risk the monitor wins and the motion stops. URML declares the goal, the speed ceiling, and the separation volume; the controller does the continuous adaptation inside those bounds. Whether the dynamic speed itself should be a URML-visible bounded parameter or stay entirely in the controller is a genuine open question, and a good one.

**On TurtleBot4 and your TB5-WaLI clone.** Right instinct. The GoPiGo3 example uses a native, non-ROS adapter because the GoPiGo3 is simplest that way. A ROS 2 robot is a different and arguably better fit for the ROS 2 reference runtime: the `RclpyAdapter` speaks the full substrate Protocol over `rclpy`, with Nav2 for navigation and MoveIt 2 for arms, and there is a gated end-to-end job that runs a TurtleBot 4 plus Nav2 in simulation against it. Your clone would map onto that path, `move_to` a Nav2 goal, rather than the `drive` / `turn` primitives the frameless GoPiGo3 uses. The code is in `reference/ros2-runtime`. If it would help, I can sketch a TurtleBot4-shaped manifest and a small program that lowers `move_to` onto a Nav2 goal, the way I did for the GoPiGo3.

You are pushing on exactly the parts that matter. Thank you for thinking out loud here.

Thanks,
Ido

> `move_to` onto a Nav2 goal

Now it gets intense - the “move_to” that WaLi has been dreaming of: move_to(pose, precision, use_rotation_shim(trigger_angle) , pause_for_moving_obstacles, replan_or_plan_once), report(pose, accuracy, duration, # recoveries and time spent in recoveries)

WaLI's dream move_to is a great test of where the line sits, so I built two things off it (PR #552).

First, a TurtleBot4 example: examples/turtlebot4/. It is the ROS 2 counterpart to the GoPiGo3 one. A mapped robot, so the program is move_to a named pose, and the ROS 2 runtime lowers that to a Nav2 NavigateToPose. Same validate-before-actuate, different substrate, no rewrite. Your WaLI clone maps onto exactly this.

Now to your move_to wishlist, because it splits into two piles, and the split is the whole design.

The substrate-neutral pile, which can be URML-visible: where to go (the pose), and arguably how close is "arrived" (precision / tolerance, since every mapped base has that notion).

The Nav2 pile, which stays out of the program: use_rotation_shim and its trigger angle, pause_for_moving_obstacles, replan_or_plan_once. Those are Nav2 controller and planner concepts. If move_to carried them, move_to would stop being implementable on a frameless GoPiGo3 or a drone, and the one-program-many-robots property is the whole point. So they live in the ROS 2 adapter's deployment config, the same place the OPC UA and Isaac adapters keep their substrate detail. WaLI's operator tunes them once for WaLI; the URML program stays portable.

Your report wishlist is the better half, and it pointed me at a real gap. report(pose, accuracy, duration, recoveries, time in recoveries) is exactly the structured run telemetry URML does not standardize today. I wrote it up as RFC-0638 (Spec, Draft, in the same PR): an optional, runtime-neutral execution contract for cancel, progress with a step identifier, and a run report that carries per-step outcomes, a duration, and a free-form telemetry map where Nav2's recovery count and recovery time would land. URML cannot define "recoveries" as a universal concept, it is meaningless on a drone, but it can give the runtime a predictable envelope to hand it back in. Your pause / resume / cancel question is the lifecycle half of the same RFC.

It is a Draft with open questions, including the precision-on-move_to one above, which is the single place your Nav2 list legitimately touches the language. If you have a view on any of them, that is exactly the input the RFC wants.

WaLI is dreaming about the right things.

Thanks,
Ido

> a TurtleBot4 example: examples/turtlebot4/

This is very emotional for me.  WaLI - (<ins>Wa</ins>llfollower <ins>L</ins>ooking for <ins>I</ins>ntelligence) thirsts for new capabilities and higher levels of "contemplation about robot thinking".

WaLI was conceived during the iRobot Create3 Software Simulation Open Beta in October 2021.  

WaLI was "re-incarnated and died"  two times on vendor hardware.  WaLI's first hardware instantiation was very briefly on the just released TurtleBot4.  (Returned due to severe cosmetic damage in shipment.)

Next WaLI attempted to materialize as a "vision only - no LIDAR" ROS 2 robot over an iRobot Create3 with a "smart camera" (Oak-D-Lite).  His Raspberry Pi brain and my "autonomous means only onboard processing" constraint quickly showed WaLI's dream was beyond his hardware without LIDAR.  This incarnation also exposed a "near death" flaw in the Create3 design and processing resources.  I spent three months working with the iRobot team to find an antidote, eventually returning WaLI's Create3 to iRobot.  After more time, the ClearPath release of the Create3 Topic Republisher for the TB4 isolated the Create3 from non-relevant message traffic.  

The Create3 topic republisher enabled WaLI's current "re-incarnation" (with both vision and LIDAR).  WaLI's most recent adventures have been "testing robustness and reliability of a 10 location tour" which can form a basis for a "mind + URML" implementation:
- Immediate fail if /battery_state.percentage < 0.4
- Immediate fail if /dock_status.is_docked == true
- Attempt /dock, fail or continue on result
- Issue /reset_pose service call  (Create3 can only reset pose to [0,0,0,w:1]  so must be on dock)
- Launch Localization
- Launch Nav2 fail if any planners fail full activation
- Issue /undock
- Announce "moving to nav ready location", wait 5, move_to(ready_for_nav_loc), announce "ready to navigate"  <- first URML "program"
- Pass the current location name and goal location name into a parameterized URML program?   <- second URML ???
  - Fail if /battery_state.percentage < 0.3  
  - Announce "Navigating from ${current_loc} to ${goal_loc}", 
  - wait 5, 
  - move_to(${goal_loc}), 
    - success: Announce "Successful navigation to ${goal_loc} within ${result.accuracy.distance} centimeters and ${resutl.accuracy.dheading} degrees" 
      - wait 20,    (for CPU load to return to baseline) 
      - Announce "ready to navigate"
      - return "results" 
    - failure: Announce "Unsuccessful navigation to ${goal_loc} goal, after ${result.retries} retries"    
      - wait 5,  
      - Announce "Be aware current location is unknown.  Requires special planning"
      - return "results"
 - If success:   current_loc = prior $goal_loc, goal_loc = next from "tour locations name list"
   - repeat parameterized "Navigate from ${current_loc} to ${goal_loc} URML program"
 - If failure: execute "move to nav ready location" URML program 
   - if failure: execute "check dock visibility, announce ready or shout 'need manual docking assistance' (honors quiet hours)
- shutdown Navigation and Localization

   
   Note use of a parameterized "Navigate from {valid named location} to {valid named location}"  to eliminate need for N-minus-1-combinations of [from-to-named-location, ...]
   
The hard part for WaLI in all this is not organizing the intent, it is managing failures.  There are some locations {Laundry_room_view, patio_window_view, next_to_dining_room_mirror} that are frightfully unreliable goal locations, and often "fly-trap" from-locations that probably only a "genetic learning navigation module" could make reliable and robust.

And I have to mention that while navigation is in progress, I cannot issue any command line ROS queries (the discovery server will  disturb navigation processing) causing the nav2 controller to throw-up all over WaLI.

Note also the need in the Announce for units conversion from radians to degrees, and meters to centimeters.  I'm not sure about the Nav2 navigation error quantization - I think it might be [dx, dy, dz, dQuaturnian] which I as the human cannot grok without conversion to "r-dTheta". I guess just like the LLM is responsible for Human to URML, the results probably need a URML-result to Human translator - small LLM or purpose built method.

WaLI's history deserves that telling, and the tour you sketched is the real test, so let me map it onto the line we have been drawing.

**Most of your tour is the mastermind, and that is correct.** The battery and dock gates, `reset_pose`, launching localization and Nav2, the undock, even "I cannot run a CLI query while nav is live" and the fly-trap locations: those are autonomy and runtime. URML expresses none of them. What is left, and what URML is for, is the inner loop you already isolated: announce, wait, `move_to(goal)`, then branch on the result to announce success or failure and return. That loop is a clean URML `sequence` with an `on_error` policy, and your tour is that program run once per leg.

**Failure management being the hard part is the right instinct.** That is where URML actually helps you, not with cleverness but with structure. Every behavior runs under `on_error` (`abort_and_report`, `continue`, `retry`), and the run result hands back `steps_executed`, an audit log of exactly which primitives ran, and the last outcome. The richer half you want, accuracy and duration and retry count coming back in a predictable shape, is precisely what RFC-0638 scopes. Your `${result.accuracy.distance}` and `${result.retries}` are the run report's per-step telemetry, so your wishlist is a direct input to that draft.

**Your parameterized "Navigate from ${a} to ${b}" is the sharpest point in the post.** You are right that you do not want N-minus-1 hand-written programs. URML today gives you binding references (`$var` from a prior `store_as`) and a `call_program` hatch, but a first-class reusable URML behavior you invoke with named arguments that substitute into the fields is not something the language defines yet. It should. You just wrote the motivating example for it, and I am going to treat it as a real design question rather than wave at the hatch.

**The radians-to-degrees, meters-to-centimeters point is subtle and good.** You have spotted the output bridge. Just as an LLM turns a human sentence into URML on the way in, a run result needs rendering on the way out, with units a person can hold. My view is that URML keeps the report structured and machine readable, distances in meters, headings in radians, no quantization opinion baked in, and the human rendering, including your quaternion to r and dTheta, lives one layer up, the natural reverse direction of the LLM bridge or a small purpose built renderer. The language stays honest about numbers; the presentation layer makes them grokkable.

If you want to push on the parameterized program or the report shape, RFC-0638 is open with exactly those questions, including whether goal precision belongs on `move_to`. WaLI is dreaming about the right things, and a couple of them are now on URML's design table because of it.

Thanks,
Ido

> "Navigate from ${a} to ${b}"

Thinking about this more - I'm not seeing the absolute need for the "from" information by the move_to(goal_loc).  My purpose was to include more functionality in the URML programs.  The continual reduction of the "URML Program Content" keeps raising organizational complexity and bifurcating the robot programming.  Complex logic goes here, simple logic goes there, but since the simpler logic can rarely be a complete expression of real robot intent, packaging robot functionality beneath another layer might just be constraining a robot vendor to box in the actual usability of the robot hardware with the layer above the URML having to set the nav2 parameters below the URML to parameterize the URML,(which invalidates the safety contract).

There seems no way "move to laundry room" could be simplified to be certified as a reusable, safe "urml mini program" (in my home, with my robot's cognitive navigation abilities).  

I'm starting to feel my sinuses filling up with the complexity of reality.  I got into ROS hoping someone else offered simplifications for my robots, and keep finding that a grammar expression of human-robot interface is the best means of expressing human intent for the robot to the robot, and my dream of a robot having purposes that it self-generates intents to fulfil is way beyond my programming or integration abilities, and the abilities of the resources I am willing to call "an autonomous robot"

I keep getting in deep and realizing I need to stay in the shallow end of the robot pool.

Two things, because you are right about one and I want to be precise about the other.

**You are right about "from."** `move_to(goal)` navigates from wherever the robot is. Nav2 owns the current pose, so passing "from" buys you nothing. That actually shrinks the parameterized-program case I got excited about: the only real argument is the destination, and a tour is then "invoke navigate(to) once per stop." Worth knowing the idea is smaller than it looked, and you are the one who found that, not me.

**The safety-contract worry is the important point, so let me be exact.** The contract URML makes is narrow: a validated program cannot command the robot outside its declared capabilities and its safety envelope, the speed ceiling, the keep-out zones, the separation volume. Those are in the program's envelope, they are checked before it runs, and a conformant runtime enforces them as a hard ceiling. Nav2's rotation shim, replan policy, and obstacle-pause tune how well the robot chases the goal inside that ceiling. They cannot raise the ceiling. A runtime that let adapter config loosen the envelope would simply be non-conformant, the same way a compiler that ignored your types would not be a compiler.

So tuning Nav2 does not invalidate the safety contract, because it cannot reach it. What you have correctly put your finger on is the real cost: the envelope is guaranteed portable and safe, but the exact motion is not. The behavior is split across layers, and that is more organizational complexity than "one program says everything." That trade is real. URML buys you a safe, checkable boundary and portability of intent; it does not buy you a single complete expression of every behavioral nuance, and I should not pretend it does.

**And the honest part.** I have spent this whole thread telling you "that lives in autonomy, that lives in the runtime, that lives in adapter config." I understand why that feels like death by a thousand cuts to the URML program. The plain truth is that URML's slice is small on purpose: it is the safe verb, not the brain. For your tour, the brain is yours, and most of the cleverness stays yours. That is not you misunderstanding the layers. That is the layers being honest about how little belongs in the safe-and-portable box.

You reached the real insight yourself a few lines up: a grammar for expressing human intent to a robot is the durable thing. The self-purposing robot that generates its own intents is hard for everyone, not a gap in your skills. There is no shame in the shallow end. A robot that reliably runs a ten-stop tour and tells you honestly when it failed is a genuinely hard, genuinely good robot, and it does not need to dream to be worth building.

WaLI has had a longer and more interesting life than most robots that cost ten times as much. Keep him moving.

Ido

> WaLI has had a longer and more interesting life than most robots that cost ten times as much. Keep him moving. For sure: ``` *** TB5-WaLI TOTAL LIFE STATISTICS *** Total Awake: 12565.5 hrs Total Naps: 0 hrs Total Life: 12565.5 hrs (since Jan 09, 2025) "Noticed Dockings": 90 Playtimes (Undocked-Docked): 2375 Total Dockings: 2465 Average playtime (last five) 1.5 hrs Average docked time (last two) 2.2 hrs Sessions (boot): 96 Average Session: 130.8 hrs Safety Shutdowns: 5 Total Travel: 6725.0 meters 22063.6 feet Last Docking: 2026-06-26 13:14|wali_node.py| ** WaLI dock goal result - Docking: success at battery 19% after 1.5 hrs playtime ** Last Recharge: 2026-06-26 15:33|wali_node.py| ** WaLI Undocking: success at battery 100%, docked for 2.3 hrs ** 15:41:14 up 49 days, 20:16, 5 users, load average: 0.18, 0.35, 0.41 ```

12,565 hours and 6.7 kilometers, with five safety shutdowns that all did their job. That is not a robot dreaming about intelligence. That is a robot living a life and keeping its own honest log of it.

Those stats are the answer to the whole thread. The good robot is the one that runs, docks, recharges, and tells you the truth about all of it, and WaLI clearly does. Forty-nine days of uptime on a Pi brain is its own kind of bragging rights.

Give him a recharge from me.

Ido

nodes.title: First GoPiGo3 Robot Runs "Validated Safe" URML Program

nodes.body:
This made my day. Lyrical-Dave is the first robot anywhere to run a validated URML program, and I love that he did it before you finished your coffee.

You also found a real bug, and an embarrassing one for a project whose whole pitch is validate before actuate: the example drove your robot when you typed -h. That is on me. A demo should never surprise-move a robot, least of all this one.

Fixed in PR #543:
- The script is now a dry run by default. A bare run, or -h, validates and prints the planned wheel and speech calls and moves nothing.
- To actually drive the wheels you pass --execute, which prints a warning first. It still auto-detects the real easygopigo3, but only when you opt in, and with no code to edit.

So now ./run_gopigo3.py -h does what habit expects, and ./run_gopigo3.py --execute is the "let Dave loose" button.

On the silence: that was a gap too. The default speech backend is espeak, and if espeak is missing or the Pi has no audio out, it said nothing and gave you nothing to debug. It now prints on stderr when it cannot speak. Better still, Dave already has a say node, so pass your own speak callback and route "announce" through it, no espeak needed:

    GoPiGo3Adapter(speak=lambda text: dave_say(text))

Thank you for running it for real, footgun and all. That is the first time the whole loop, English to validated program to a robot actually moving, has closed outside my own machine. Dave earned the Mastodon post.

Thanks,
Ido

@slowrunner this is going up on urml.dev as a field note, crediting you and Dave. As last time, here is the near-final before it goes live, so you can change anything, especially anything about you or Dave.

It reuses the Lyrical-Dave photo you shared, credits you as @slowrunner with links to your LyricalDave repo and your Mastodon post, and it is honest that the footgun was ours, not yours.

---


This week a community member who goes by [@slowrunner](https://github.com/slowrunner) closed the loop the whole project is built around. An English sentence, validated into a robot program, executed on real hardware. His GoPiGo3, Lyrical-Dave, drove across the room. Then it drove under a chair.

![Lyrical-Dave, a GoPiGo3 ROS 2 robot](/blog/lyrical-dave.jpg)

*Lyrical-Dave, @slowrunner's GoPiGo3 ROS 2 robot. Photo: @slowrunner.*

## The headline

This is the first time the full URML loop has run end to end outside a maintainer's machine: English, to a validated program, to a robot that moves, on an educational two-wheel buggy and a Raspberry Pi, with no cloud. The loop closed on someone else's robot, in their own home. That is the milestone.

## How it actually happened, which is the better story

We had just shipped an update to the GoPiGo3 example so it would notice a real robot and use it. @slowrunner pulled the update onto Dave, copied the example into his test folder, and ran it with `-h`, out of habit, expecting a help message. Instead he heard motors in the next room. He raced in to find Dave spinning ninety degrees and heading under a chair, his heart, in his words, racing as fast as Dave's.

He told it himself, with good humor: be careful what you type, your robot may be listening.

## The part we are not proud of, and fixed

URML's entire pitch is validate before actuate. Nothing moves until it is checked. And our own example moved a robot when someone typed `-h`. That is precisely the failure the project exists to prevent, and we had built it into the demo.

So we fixed it the same day. The example is now a dry run by default. Run it, or run it with `-h`, and it validates the program and prints the wheel and speech commands it would issue, and moves nothing. To actually drive the robot you pass `--execute`, which warns you first. Actuation is opt-in, the way it should have been from the start.

The lesson is the project's own, turned back on itself: a validated-safe program is only safe if running the tool cannot surprise you into executing it. The gate has to sit in front of the motor, including in the demo.

## What the robot was actually told

The "validated safe" program Dave ran was a short patrol: announce, drive a meter, turn, drive, return home. Every step had been checked against Dave's declared capabilities, a frameless two-wheel buggy with wheel encoders, before a single wheel turned. The validator did its job. The demo's invocation did not. Now both do.

One footnote: Dave moved but stayed silent. The example's default speech path is espeak, and on Dave it produced no sound and, worse, no error. That was a gap too, so the adapter now says on its log when it cannot speak, and a robot with its own voice, like Dave's ROS say node, can be wired straight in.

## Why we are writing this down

The validator-first design held: the robot did only what was declared possible and checked safe. What failed was operational glue around the demo, and a user caught it on his own hardware in the most memorable way possible. That is what early adoption looks like, and it is worth more than a clean launch.

The full thread, including Dave's own account, is on the discussion board. Lyrical-Dave's code is at [github.com/slowrunner/LyricalDave](https://github.com/slowrunner/LyricalDave).

---

If that reads right to you, it goes live. Anything to fix, just say and I will change it.

Thanks,
Ido

The description of "patrol" is not accurate - and including the urml can create a "teaching moment" 

```
        "profile": ["educational"],
        "behavior": {
            "type": "sequence",
            "on_error": "abort_and_report",
            "steps": [
                {"turn": {"angle": 90}},
                {"drive": {"distance": 0.5}},
                {"turn": {"angle": -90}},
                {"drive": {"distance": 0.5}},
                {"speak": {"utterance": "Patrol complete"}},
                {"report": {"to": "run_log", "facts": {"patrol": "done"}, "status": "success"}},
            ],

```

otherwise "ready for pub".  Dave is onto his next adventure learning to express himself in the "Universal" robot language.

Good catch, and thank you. That is exactly the kind of error I want caught before it sits on the site. You are right: it was turn ninety, drive half a meter, turn back, drive half a meter, announce, report, not "drive a meter and return home." Corrected (PR #41).

I also took your teaching-moment suggestion and put the actual program in the post, in full, with a line on what the validator checked against Dave's manifest before any wheel turned. One real URML program on the page is worth more than my prose describing it.

So it is fixed and going live with the URML shown, credited to you for the catch. Thank you for reading it that closely.

Enjoy Dave's next adventure in the universal robot language.

Thanks,
Ido

nodes.title: [Idea] Strongly Visible "Install / Update" page?

nodes.body:
Good catch, and you are right that "how do I update" should not be a hunt.
I added an "Updating an existing install" note to the README quickstart (PR #532):

    . .venv/bin/activate
    pip install --upgrade urml-validator urml-ros2-runtime urml-llm-bridge
    urml --version

That is the path to pick up a new flag like --save-rejected.
pipx upgrade urml-validator does the same for a pipx install.

Two of four clean, with one structural failure and one malformed-JSON failure, on a 1.5B model. That's the capability wall showing its texture: at this size it's roughly a coin flip, and the failures split exactly the two ways we talked about.

The 2nd run was structural (it invented `behavior/step/sequence` nesting). The 4th was pure formatting, since "Expecting ',' delimiter" is broken JSON, not bad intent. That 4th one is the case for a JSON-cleanup pass, so if `--save-rejected` catches a few like it, send them over.

On the statistics: you don't really need them. What matters is the success rate, and with this much run-to-run variance you won't engineer a 1.5B model to reliable. Ten or twenty runs would pin the rate, but the rate is the wrong thing to chase here.

Here's what makes it not matter: translate once, run forever. The reason translate and execute are split is exactly so you aren't the model's tester on every run. Get one clean `program.urml.yaml` and that file is yours, deterministic and validated, reusable offline with no model in the loop. The flaky part happens once, at authoring time, and the validator refuses anything malformed before it reaches the robot. You're the author with a gate, not the tester of an oracle.

And the part you'll want: the relative-motion verbs you asked for just landed. `drive { distance, arc }` and `turn { angle }` are in URML now (RFC-0630), gated to the educational profile and a `supports_relative_motion` flag on the manifest. Here's a working starting point for the GoPiGo3 manifest, so you don't have to fight the schema.

It validates as-is. Frameless, dead reckoning, two encoders, a speaker:

```yaml
manifest_version: "0.1"
robot_id: gopigo3
description: GoPiGo3 Raspberry Pi educational robot. Two motors with wheel encoders and a speaker. Frameless dead reckoning, local floor frame.

frames:
  - name: floor
    parent: null
  - name: base_link
    parent: floor

mobility:
  drive_type: differential
  max_velocity: 0.30
  supports_relative_motion: true
  max_relative_distance: 3.0

outputs:
  named_endpoints:
    - speech
```

And the "announce, then execute" pattern you described, as a program that validates against it:

```yaml
profile: educational
behavior:
  type: sequence
  on_error: abort_and_report
  steps:
    - speak: { utterance: "Preparing to drive forward half a meter." }
    - drive: { distance: 0.5 }
    - speak: { utterance: "Preparing to spin left ninety degrees." }
    - turn: { angle: 90 }
```

A few notes so it makes sense:

The `speak` steps need `speech` in `outputs.named_endpoints` (it's there). `drive` / `turn` need `supports_relative_motion: true` plus the `educational` profile (both there). Distance is metres, so Layer 4 turns "a foot" into 0.3048; angle is degrees, and positive is counterclockwise / left, so a right turn is a negative angle.

Now the part that would actually close your loop.

You can translate and validate today, but there's no GoPiGo3 runtime adapter yet, so a validated program doesn't drive the wheels. That's the missing piece between "valid YAML" and Carl actually moving.

Want to build a GoPiGo3 adapter together? URML has done this for a few other small robots (Marty, Petoi, a CircuitPython board): a thin adapter that maps the primitives onto the robot's own API. For the GoPiGo3 that's roughly drive -> a drive-cm / encoder target, turn -> turn-degrees, speak -> the speaker. I'd write the adapter; you'd point me at the exact GoPiGo3 API calls you use and test it on the real robot, since you're the one with it on the desk. That's the fastest path to your Pi translating an English sentence and the GoPiGo3 doing it.

No pressure either way. Drop the GoPiGo3 API details here and I'll start, or just take the manifest and keep experimenting.

Thanks,
Ido

> you can drop the LLM entirely. That's the part I don't think came across. URML is meant to be human-writable; the natural-language front door is one optional way in, not the way in.

Correct, and if your URML definition were to become a standard, TheConstruct and Udemy could create a new class of robot programmers that do not need to learn to configure the 200 parameters of ROS 2 Nav2 to get the bot from the dock to the kitchen.  Even better than C++ students not needing to debug at the  C++ runtime level.  (Note: Even Claude wasn't able to make my TurtleBot4 robot "TB5-WaLI" reliably follow_waypoints to/from 10 "stations" in my home.  Took me down so many rabbit holes on the way, I had to give up and settle for a human optimization.)

From my POV, "vibe coding" is all the rage, and most people seem to think it is a starting path to wrangling devices.  Your URML as an "embedded grammar" and program validator is the only way untrained people should be allowed to talk to their devices.  It has always been the case that coding was the simplest part of building systems.  The architecture design, the software implementation design, the test design, the validation design, and of course the most important success factor - the marketing design are totally missed by most neophyte "vibe-coders".

All my robots are custom designs with no high-level transferable skills (or learned knowledge).  Humans transfer knowledge and skills.  The integrated circuit raised the level of design from individual components to modules.  ROS  is attempting to raise the design process from custom nodes, topics, services, etc. to whole packages we can pull together, but the packages are too flexible, too complex, and very fast moving targets.  The biennial  LTS ROS release is where we were before Continuous Integration and updates from the cloud, but either make robot vendor maintenance a serious commitment that the market has not valued yet.

So bottom line, as a former interactive voice response designer/coder/tester I am still looking for the "singularity" that allows verbal NLU to the nearly infinite combinations of a finite set of sensors and effectors (and processing resource).  Lots of folks have been wrapping LLMs with MCP frameworks and agents.  URML is the first, easy for me to understand, wrangler of these wildly creative (hallucinatory) black boxes that each wants to be a base module people will agree on.

My other investigation right now is to learn behavior trees with a blackboard with the goal to convert my ROS robots from state machines to BTs.  My exposure to your URML may offer another programming modality for my robots, so I'm sticking around to see how it all develops.

This is the most useful kind of feedback, thank you. You're seeing it from exactly the angle I built it from.

The IVR parallel is the one I'd reach for too. A voice-response system works because the grammar is bounded and every input is validated against what the system can actually do before anything happens. URML is that discipline pointed at physical action: a bounded vocabulary, validated against the robot's real capabilities, before a motor turns. The LLM is just a fancier way to fill the grammar, held to the same contract.

Your TB4 / follow_waypoints story is the whole motivation in one example. "Dock to kitchen" should be one declared intent against a manifest, not 200 Nav2 parameters and a week of rabbit holes. URML's move_to is exactly that: declare the location, the validator confirms it's reachable and declared, and Nav2 owns the 200 knobs underneath. You shouldn't have to debug at that layer to get a robot across a room.

On behavior trees, there's a real connection worth knowing. URML's Layer 3 is behavior composition: sequence, branch, parallel, retry, with error handling. It's deliberately BT-adjacent, but a level up: URML is the declarative, validated intent, and a behavior tree is one of the things it can lower to (BehaviorTree.CPP is a target; a FlexBE state machine is another). So your BT work and URML aren't competing modalities. URML can be the layer that decides what the tree should do, checked before it runs, while the tree handles the reactive execution. If you go down the BT-with-blackboard path, that seam is where URML would plug in.

No pressure on any of it. "Sticking around to see how it develops" is exactly the right posture, and I'd rather have a sharp skeptic watching than a fan. The GoPiGo adapter offer stays open whenever you want to move Carl; the manifest's there to hand-write against in the meantime.

Thanks,
Ido

> BehaviorTree.CPP is a target;

I'm using BehaviorTree.ROS2 which works in Jazzy, Kilted, and Lyrical Luth.  

Lyrical-Dave is my ROS 2 GoPiGo3 bot that is "learning BTs, and lifecycle nodes" 
(and "teaching Claude" to use multi-threaded executors with reentrant callback groups instead of creating ROS slop.)

First Use Case:
- Uses existing VOSKROS node with speech reco grammar (to blackboard)
- Existing dave/say_node produces text-to-speech output BT endpoint
   - allows volume 
   - allows "speak anytime" flag to ignore quiet hours 11pm to 10am for testing. 
      (Carl taught me safety shutdown is better than shouting "Help! Need Manual Docking Assistance" in the middle of the night.) 
   - logs every speak request tagged with datetime and -spoken or -quiettime to speak.log
- non-repeating random greeting response BT endpoint
- battery_state service (from blackboard) BT endpoint
- specific greeting to specific response BT endpoints
- random class greetings (hi dave, hey dave, ...) to random greeting response BT endpoints
- battery state request to battery_state service BT endpoints
- "Go To Sleep Dave" restricts BT to "Wake Up Dave" endpoint
- Log every accepted utterance to heard.log with datetime

(Current functionality in progress - Mute speech reco to the blackboard during speech output to prevent self excitation by out of grammar utterances since speech reco engine has no pause API)
  
```
(gopigo3) ubuntu@U26LDave:~/LyricalDave/ros2ws/params$ more bt_hello_dave_tree.xml 
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<root BTCPP_format="4" main_tree_to_execute="MainTree">

  <!-- ======================================================================
       MAIN TREE
       Three parallel branches, all must keep running (ParallelAll):
         1. STT result subscriber  -> pushes onto stt_queue blackboard
         2. Battery state subscriber -> updates battery_state blackboard
         3. HelloDave dialog subtree -> matches grammar & responds
  ======================================================================= -->
  <BehaviorTree ID="MainTree">
    <ParallelAll>

      <KeepRunningUntilFailure>
        <SttResultSubscriber topic_name="/stt/result"/>
      </KeepRunningUntilFailure>

      <KeepRunningUntilFailure>
        <BatteryStateSubscriber topic_name="/battery_state"/>
      </KeepRunningUntilFailure>

      <SubTree ID="HelloDaveDialog"/>

    </ParallelAll>
  </BehaviorTree>


  <!-- ======================================================================
       HELLO DAVE DIALOG SUBTREE
       Repeats forever. Each tick tries (in order):
         1. Match newest single stt_queue entry against grammar
         2. Match oldest pair of entries (split-phrase across two messages)
         3. If queue stale/full and nothing matched, discard oldest entry
         4. Otherwise do nothing this tick
  ======================================================================= -->
  <BehaviorTree ID="HelloDaveDialog">
    <Repeat num_cycles="-1">
      <ReactiveFallback>

        <!-- Branch 1: single newest entry -->
        <Sequence>
          <CheckSttQueueNonEmpty/>
          <MatchGrammar window="1"
                        matched_phrase="{matched_phrase}"
                        consumed_count="{consumed_count}"/>
          <SubTree ID="DispatchResponse"
                   matched_phrase="{matched_phrase}"
                   consumed_count="{consumed_count}"/>
        </Sequence>

        <!-- Branch 2: oldest pair (split phrase) -->
        <Sequence>
          <CheckSttQueueSize min_size="2"/>
          <MatchGrammar window="2"
                        matched_phrase="{matched_phrase}"
                        consumed_count="{consumed_count}"/>
          <SubTree ID="DispatchResponse"
                   matched_phrase="{matched_phrase}"
                   consumed_count="{consumed_count}"/>
        </Sequence>

        <!-- Branch 3: nothing matched -> discard stale/full entry -->
        <Sequence>
          <CheckSttQueueStaleOrFull/>
          <RemoveSttEntries count="1"/>
        </Sequence>

        <!-- Branch 4: nothing to do -->
        <AlwaysSuccess/>

      </ReactiveFallback>
    </Repeat>
  </BehaviorTree>


  <!-- ======================================================================
       DISPATCH RESPONSE SUBTREE
       Given a matched_phrase + consumed_count:
         - LogHeard always fires first (every in-grammar match is logged,
           awake or asleep).
         - CheckSleepModeBlocksResponse then gates the actual response:
           if Dave is asleep and the phrase isn't "wake up dave", the
           response Fallback is skipped entirely; the phrase was
           logged but not acted upon.
         - Otherwise, dispatch as before:
             - Fixed, no-processing phrases -> SayFixed directly (data-driven
               from YAML "responses.fixed" map, read inside SayFixed node)
             - Greeting phrases -> SayRandomGreeting (anti-repeat picker)
             - Battery phrase -> BuildBatteryReport + SayService
       In all cases: remove consumed entries at the end.
  ======================================================================= -->
  <BehaviorTree ID="DispatchResponse">
    <Sequence>

      <LogHeard phrase="{matched_phrase}"/>

      <Fallback>

        <!-- Asleep and not "wake up dave": suppress response, but the
             phrase has already been logged above. -->
        <CheckSleepModeBlocksResponse phrase="{matched_phrase}"/>

        <!-- Awake, or "wake up dave" while asleep: normal dispatch -->
        <Fallback>

          <!-- Greeting phrases: random anti-repeat response -->
          <Sequence>
            <CheckPhraseInList phrase="{matched_phrase}" list_key="greeting_phrases"/>
            <SayRandomGreeting/>
          </Sequence>

          <!-- Battery report: built from blackboard battery_state -->
          <Sequence>
            <CheckPhraseInList phrase="{matched_phrase}" list_key="battery_phrases"/>
            <BuildBatteryReport report_text="{report_text}"/>
            <SayService saystring="{report_text}" volume="50" anytime="true"
                         service_name="/say"/>
          </Sequence>

          <!-- Everything else: fixed phrase/response from YAML "fixed" map -->
          <Sequence>
            <SayFixed phrase="{matched_phrase}" service_name="/say"/>
          </Sequence>

        </Fallback>

      </Fallback>

      <RemoveSttEntries count="{consumed_count}"/>

    </Sequence>
  </BehaviorTree>

</root>

```

That's a well-built tree. The sleep gate that still logs, the split-phrase window, the anti-repeat greeting, the self-excitation mute, those are the details that separate a demo from something you actually live with. Carl teaching you that safety shutdown beats shouting at 3am is the best kind of requirement.

Let me be precise about where URML fits, including where it doesn't.

Your dialog loop is exactly right as a behavior tree, and URML should not touch it. Always-listening, match grammar, respond, gate on sleep mode: that's reactive control, and a BT with a blackboard is the correct tool. URML's composition layer is for building a task, not running a perpetual reactive dialog, so expressing your MainTree in URML would be using the wrong layer.

Where URML earns a place is one branch inside DispatchResponse. Right now a matched phrase routes to a greeting, a battery report, or a fixed response. Add one more class: phrases that are physical-task commands. "Drive to the kitchen and come back." "Patrol the four corners." Those don't have a fixed response; they have an intent that has to be checked against what Dave can actually do, then executed. That's URML's job: a RunUrmlProgram node, sibling to your SayService and SayFixed, that takes the intent, validates it against Dave's manifest, and runs the validated program, returning success or failure up the tree like any other node.

So the split is clean. The BT owns the conversation and the reactive loop. URML owns what the robot physically does, and whether it's possible and safe before it moves. Your VOSK grammar bounds what Dave will hear; URML's validator bounds what Dave will do. Two gates, two layers, the same discipline you already trust.

And the part that should appeal to you: your grammar is already a deterministic natural-language front end. For a movement command you don't need the LLM at all, you can map the matched phrase straight to a URML program, hand-written or templated, and execute it. The flaky black box never enters the picture. That's the version I'd actually run on a robot I cared about.

If you ever want that RunUrmlProgram node, it's the GoPiGo adapter plus a thin BT wrapper, and I'd build it from the EasyGoPiGo3 calls you gave me. No rush. This is a good place to be thinking from.

Thanks,
Ido

**Field notes: running URML on a Raspberry Pi with a local LLM**

A community member who goes by @slowrunner spent a few days running URML on a Raspberry Pi 5, translating plain English into validated robot programs with a local model through Ollama. No cloud, no subscription, everything on the robot. The whole exchange happened in the open on our discussion board, and it taught us more than a month of planning would have.

*[photo of Lyrical-Dave here] — Lyrical-Dave, @slowrunner's GoPiGo3 ROS 2 robot. Photo: @slowrunner.*

**The headline**

A 986 MB model (qwen2.5:1.5b) running locally on the Pi, at a 32k context, translated "drive around the four corners of the room and come back home" into a valid URML program. Accepted on the first try, no revisions, entirely on a 4 GB single-board computer.

That is the "under 2 GB on the edge" case people keep asking about, and it works. With one large caveat.

**The honest part**

Small models are not reliable at this. The same prompt, same machine, same model gave a clean program on some runs and a malformed one on others. At 1.5 billion parameters it is closer to a coin flip than a tool, and the failures split two ways: structural, where the model invents fields or nests them wrong, and formatting, where the intent is right but the JSON is broken.

This is exactly why URML splits translation from execution. The flaky, model-shaped step happens once, at authoring time, behind a validator that refuses anything malformed before it reaches the robot. You translate once, get a validated program, and that file is yours: deterministic, offline, reusable with no model in the loop. You are the author with a gate, not the tester of an oracle.

**What the exchange shipped**

Real use surfaced real gaps, and four of them closed in a few days:

- `urml translate --save-rejected` writes the model's final rejected output to a file, marked do-not-execute, so you can see exactly what a small model produced when it failed.
- `drive` and `turn` (RFC-0630): relative-motion primitives for frameless robots, the "drive forward a foot, spin ninety degrees" vocabulary a wheel-encoder buggy actually speaks.
- Educational few-shots so the bridge can teach a small model to emit those new verbs.
- A conservative JSON-repair pass that recovers an otherwise-valid program wrapped in a Markdown fence, surrounded by prose, or carrying a trailing comma. The validator still gates the result, so repair can only recover a good program, never admit a bad one.

**Why we are writing this down**

This is what early adoption looks like, and it is not a number on a dashboard. It is one person using the thing for real, on cheap hardware, and pulling features out of it by hitting honest limits. The validator-first design is the part that held up: a small model can be as creative or as wrong as it likes, and the robot still only does what was declared possible and checked safe.

These are robots someone actually lives with. Lyrical-Dave has logged over ten thousand hours since 2021 and more than two thousand dockings, and during this very exchange it rode out a 1:30 AM docking failure on its own: it retried, recovered, and never woke its owner. That is what the discipline is for, a robot that does only what was declared possible and checked safe, even at 1:30 in the morning.

The full thread, including the working Ollama setup, is on the discussion board. Lyrical-Dave's own code is at github.com/slowrunner/LyricalDave.
